title: Additive solid immersion lenses for enhanced collection efficiency of shallow NV centers by pulsed laser deposition and structurization of high-k amorphous oxides
authors: Michael S. Bar, Nicole Raatz, Max Kneiss, Andreas Koenig, Marius Grundmann, Holger von Wenckstern
abstract: The negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy ($\mathrm{NV}^-$) defect in diamond can be used for quantum information processing via the readout of the radiative decay of the excited state into the ground state. The large refractive index mismatch of diamond and air causes low photon extraction efficiency due to total internal reflection losses. Here, we investigate the photon extraction numerically and report additive solid immersion lenses (SILs) consisting of the high-k dielectric yttria-stabilized-zirconia (YSZ) for surface modification and enhanced light extraction of shallow implanted nitrogen-vacancy centers. We demonstrate an average increase of 63% in saturation intensity using a scalable bottum up room temperature pulsed laser deposition and photolithography structurization process. The average necessary laser intensity for saturation is reduced by 33% by the SILs.
summary: This paper reports on the use of Additive Solid Immersion Lenses (SILs), fabricated via Pulsed Laser Deposition of high-k oxides like YSZ, to boost the light collection efficiency from NV centers in diamond. By mitigating total internal reflection losses, the technique significantly increases the measurable saturation intensity of the quantum emitter, making it a viable platform for quantum information processing.
main_problem: The primary challenge is the low photon extraction efficiency from shallow Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV−) centers in diamond due to total internal reflection losses caused by the refractive index mismatch with air.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated that using Additive Solid Immersion Lenses (SILs) made of high-k amorphous oxides significantly enhances light collection, achieving an average 63% increase in saturation intensity.
method: The study combines numerical simulations (Monte-Carlo) to model photon extraction with experimental fabrication techniques like Pulsed Laser Deposition (PLD) and photolithography to create the SIL structures.
model_or_system: The physical system is NV− centers embedded in diamond. The enhancement mechanism involves depositing high-k dielectric materials, such as Yttria-Stabilized Zirconia (YSZ), onto the surface to act as an immersion lens.
key_observables: Photon extraction efficiency ($\eta$), saturation intensity ($I_{sat}$), and the necessary laser intensity for saturation.
important_parameters: The refractive index ($n$) of the SIL material, the lateral offset ($\Delta$) of the light source, and the SIL geometry parameters (diameter $2r$, thickness $t$).
main_assumptions: Initial simulations did not consider Fresnel reflections, and the performance is sensitive to fabrication imperfections like sidewall deposition ('fencing').
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the fabrication process, showing the array of curved SILs and cross-sections, and compare fluorescence measurements (saturation counts) under different surface conditions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the optical loss problem to simulating the theoretical enhancement using SILs, and finally validating the concept through the scalable, bottom-up fabrication and measurement of the enhanced photon collection efficiency.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical quantum optics challenge of coupling single-photon emitters to external optical circuits by engineering the local photonic environment, which is crucial for quantum networking and quantum memory.
